blocks.content: Recognize transponder purpose and basic modes.

items.definition: A squawk code is a 4-digit octal number (0000–7777, excluding some) assigned by ATC to identify a specific aircraft on radar. The transponder replies to radar interrogations with the code, allowing controllers to correlate the radar return with the specific flight.
items.analogy: Like a name badge at a conference — the squawk code tells ATC which radar blip belongs to which aircraft.

items.definition: The transponder replies to Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR) interrogations from ATC ground stations. SSR interrogates at 1030 MHz; transponder replies at 1090 MHz with squawk code and altitude. This allows ATC to positively identify and track the aircraft on radar.
items.analogy: Like a ship's IFF system — when the radar pings you, you reply with your identity code so the controller knows who you are.

items.definition: Transponder antennas operate at 1030/1090 MHz. Installation: (1) verify 50Ω impedance match, (2) use appropriate coax (low-loss type at ~1 GHz, e.g., RG-400 or similar), (3) torque TNC or BNC connectors per spec, (4) verify SWR after installation.
items.analogy: Like installing a high-frequency speaker — you need the right impedance cable and proper connections or you'll lose signal before it gets there.

items.definition: Mode S assigns each aircraft a unique 24-bit ICAO address (set during manufacture/registration). ATC systems use this to selectively interrogate specific aircraft (not all-call interrogation like Mode A/C). Enables data link, reduces RF congestion, and supports ADS-B Out transmission.
items.analogy: Like a cell phone number — it's yours alone, so the tower can call just you rather than broadcasting to everyone.

items.definition: Mode C replies include Mode A squawk code PLUS pressure altitude (Gillham code from encoding altimeter or ADC). Altitude is transmitted in 100-ft increments referenced to 29.92 inHg (standard pressure). ATC can see both aircraft identity and altitude on their display.
items.analogy: Mode A is like sending a text with just your name. Mode C is like sending your name AND your GPS altitude at the same time.

items.definition: Transponder antennas are low-profile blade or stub antennas tuned to 1030/1090 MHz (L-band). Mounted on the belly (bottom of fuselage) and/or top of fuselage. Low profile to minimize drag. 50Ω impedance.
items.analogy: Like a small shark fin on an aircraft belly — compact, low-drag, tuned to work at the specific L-band frequencies.

items.term: Mode C — combined ID and altitude
items.definition: Mode C is the standard operating mode for IFR flight, providing both Mode A squawk code (identity) and pressure altitude in a single transponder reply. Most ATC radar requires Mode C in controlled airspace above 10,000 MSL and near Class B/C airports.
items.analogy: Like sending a package with both a name label AND a return address — ATC gets both who you are and where you are vertically in one reply.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of a transponder squawk code?
choices: To encode the aircraft's altitude in binary for TCAS processing
To allow ATC radar to identify and track a specific aircraft among other traffic
To broadcast GPS position data to nearby aircraft via ADS-B
To encrypt the transponder reply to prevent spoofing
blocks.feedback: The squawk code is an identification tool — it lets ATC correlate a specific radar return with a specific flight. Without squawk, the radar shows only anonymous returns; with squawk, ATC can say 'that's N12345' and track it with callsign, altitude, and flight data attached.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of an aircraft transponder?
choices: To broadcast GPS position data to other aircraft
To encrypt aircraft identification data for security purposes
To monitor other transponder-equipped aircraft for collision avoidance
To reply to ATC secondary surveillance radar interrogations for identification and tracking
blocks.feedback: The transponder is fundamentally a reply device — it listens for SSR interrogations and responds with coded information (squawk code in Mode A, altitude in Mode C, data link in Mode S). This allows ATC secondary radar to create the labeled radar display controllers use for separation.

blocks.question: What must be verified when installing a transponder antenna?
choices: Antenna impedance match, correct coaxial cable type, and connector torque to specification
Only that the physical mounting is secure — RF performance self-adjusts
That the antenna is co-located with the VOR antenna for shared ground plane
Only the coax length — connector type doesn't matter at transponder frequencies
blocks.feedback: All three are required: impedance match ensures proper power transfer and minimal reflection; correct coax minimizes loss at ~1 GHz (standard RG-58 has too much loss); proper connector torque ensures electrical contact and weatherproofing. Ignoring any of these risks poor transponder performance or compliance failure.

blocks.question: What does the 24-bit ICAO address in a Mode S transponder enable?
choices: Encoding of aircraft registration number in audio Morse code
Selective interrogation of specific aircraft by ATC systems
Automatic frequency selection for the most congested sector
Encryption of altitude data to prevent spoofing
blocks.feedback: The 24-bit address enables selective interrogation — ATC can query a specific aircraft's transponder rather than broadcasting to all. This reduces RF congestion in busy airspace and enables two-way data link communication (used for ACAS coordination, ATIS data, and future applications).

blocks.question: What does a Mode C transponder transmit in addition to the squawk code?
choices: GPS-derived latitude and longitude position
Aircraft registration number in ICAO format
Groundspeed computed from GPS data
Pressure altitude encoded from an encoding altimeter
blocks.feedback: Mode C = Mode A (squawk code) + pressure altitude. The altitude comes from an encoding altimeter (mechanical Gillham code output) or air data computer, transmitted in 100-ft increments at standard pressure (29.92). ATC sees altitude tagged to each radar return.

blocks.question: What type of antenna does a transponder use and at what frequencies?
choices: Low-profile blade or stub antenna at 1030/1090 MHz
Loop antenna at 190–535 kHz
V-shaped bent dipole at 108–118 MHz
Patch antenna at 1575 MHz
blocks.feedback: Transponders operate in the L-band at 1030 MHz (interrogation) and 1090 MHz (reply). Low-profile blade or stub antennas are standard — they provide the omni pattern needed for ATC line-of-sight while minimizing drag. V-shaped dipoles are VOR; loops are ADF; patch antennas are GPS.

blocks.question: What combination of information does Mode C provide?
choices: GPS position and velocity only
Both the Mode A squawk code (identification) and pressure altitude reporting
Pressure altitude only, with no identification
Pilot-entered flight plan data and squawk code
blocks.feedback: Mode C = Mode A identity (squawk code) + automatic pressure altitude from encoding altimeter. This combination is what allows ATC radar displays to show both the labeled aircraft identity and its altitude — the minimum information needed for basic radar separation services.
